summary: Defines the data fields and data types for In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance, a way to record operational and telemetry information inside packets as they travel a path. The fields can be carried in several encapsulations, such as NSH, Segment Routing, Geneve, or IPv6. It complements probe-based tools like ICMP. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Each packet carries a travel diary and every stop it passes writes a note, so you can see where it was slow.

subtitle: The data fields that let each packet carry its own telemetry diary through a network domain.

tldr.problem: Probe tools such as ICMP-based Ping and Traceroute send extra packets that may be handled differently from real traffic, so they can miss what the data traffic actually experiences.
tldr.mechanism: IOAM defines data fields, grouped into four Option-Types (two kinds of trace, proof of transit, and edge-to-edge), that nodes in a limited domain add to or fill in on real packets as they travel a path.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines only the fields and registries, not how they are carried: each encapsulation (NSH, Segment Routing, Geneve, IPv6) is specified elsewhere, and any such specification MUST provide cryptographic integrity protection.

today: RFC 9197 is a Proposed Standard from May 2022, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines fields and registries only; the RFC says each encapsulation is to be specified separately.

sections.title: Why Put Telemetry Inside Packets
sections.content:
RFC 9197 defines data fields for In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (IOAM). IOAM records OAM information inside a packet while it crosses a particular network domain. "In situ" means the data is added to ordinary data packets instead of being sent in packets dedicated to OAM.

The RFC places IOAM between active and passive measurement: it adds information to packets that already exist, so it is not passive, and it needs no extra packets. In the classification of RFC 7799 it is a Hybrid Type I method.

It is meant to complement tools such as Ping and Traceroute. It helps where ICMP-based mechanisms do not apply or give poor results, for example proving that a flow takes a predefined path, checking an SLA for data traffic, getting detailed statistics on traffic spread over multiple paths, or when probe traffic is treated differently from regular data traffic.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending a scout ahead to see what the road is like, you let the real traveller keep a diary. The diary tells the truth about the actual trip.

sections.title: Scope, Limited Domains and Assumptions
sections.content:
This document defines only the data fields and their data types. How they are encapsulated in NSH, Segment Routing, Geneve or IPv6 is out of scope; each encapsulation is expected to be specified by its own RFC, jointly designed by the owning working group and the IETF IPPM Working Group. Deployment advice is also left to a separate document.

IOAM is aimed at limited domains, such as an enterprise campus or an overlay network. A limited domain may contain one or more IOAM-Domains, each told apart by namespace identifiers. The operator is expected to keep IOAM data from leaking past the edge of an IOAM-Domain, for example with packet filtering.

The operator SHOULD also think about side effects of the larger packets: load balancing based on packet length (ECMP) can be affected, the MTU of every link in the domain must be large enough (PMTU), and ICMP handling matters, since for IPv6 the RFC says IOAM support for echo request and reply is desired.

IOAM can be applied to all traffic or only to a subset, which can limit processing cost. Its fields are independent of the protocol that carries them. If tunnels are stacked, IOAM fields can exist at several layers, and each layer behaves independently, the "ships-in-the-night" model.
sections.eli5: IOAM is meant for one club or campus, not the whole world. The diary should be torn off before the postcard leaves the building, and the building needs doors wide enough for a fatter postcard.

sections.title: Nodes, Domains and Namespaces
sections.content:
An IOAM-Domain has three roles. An encapsulating node adds at least one IOAM-Option-Type to a packet. A decapsulating node removes it. Transit nodes read, write or process IOAM data in between. Not every node in a domain has to be a transit node; the RFC gives the example of only firewalls taking part. A transit node MUST ignore Option-Types it does not understand, MUST NOT add or remove Option-Types, and MUST NOT change the fields of an Edge-to-Edge Option-Type.

Roles are always played within an IOAM-Namespace, identified by a 16-bit Namespace-ID. Values 0x0001 to 0x7FFF are operator-assigned, and 0x8000 to 0xFFFF are IANA-assigned. The value 0x0000 is the Default-Namespace-ID, which every IOAM node MUST support. If a packet's Namespace-ID matches no namespace a node is configured for, the node MUST NOT change the IOAM data.

Namespaces give context. A node_id does not have to be globally unique, because node_id plus Namespace-ID is always unique. A namespace can also tell the receiver which timestamp format is used, how to read unitless fields, and which group of devices a node belongs to. Splitting devices across namespaces lets an operator rebuild a full trace from partial ones.
sections.eli5: A namespace is like the name of a game. Everyone playing the same game reads the diary the same way, and players of a different game leave it alone.

sections.title: The Trace Option-Types
sections.content:
Tracing collects a record from each node: its identity, the interfaces the packet came in and went out on, the time of day and transit delay, and free-format data such as queue or battery level. The RFC defines it as two options so both hardware and software can be efficient.

  • The Pre-allocated Trace Option reserves space for every node up front. A pointer-like value marks the next empty slot, and the array fills from the last entry backwards.
  • The Incremental Trace Option lets each node push its data right after the option header, so transit nodes need not read the whole array.

Encapsulating and decapsulating nodes that support tracing MUST support both. A transit node needs only one, and if both options are in a packet the Incremental one MUST come first.

Both share a fixed header: Namespace-ID (16 bits), NodeLen (5 bits, node data length in 4-octet units), Flags (4 bits), RemainingLen (7 bits, space left in 4-octet units), a 24-bit IOAM Trace-Type bit field and 8 reserved bits. Transit nodes may change only Flags and RemainingLen. If a node finds too little space left, it adds nothing and sets the Overflow bit (O-bit) in Flags.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of diary. In one, the pages are numbered ahead of time and each stop fills in the next blank page. In the other, each stop adds a fresh page on top.

sections.title: Node Data Fields
sections.content:
Each bit set in the Trace-Type adds one field to every node's entry, packed in bit order. All fields are aligned to 4 octets. A field a node cannot fill is set to 0xFFFFFFFF (or 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF for 8-octet fields), meaning "not populated".

Several fields come in a short format (4 octets) and a wide format (8 octets), and a deployment may use both. For example, the short interface identifier might name a physical interface while the wide one names a logical sub-interface.

  • Hop_Lim (1 octet) plus node_id (3 octets short, 7 octets wide).
  • ingress_if_id and egress_if_id (2 octets each short, 4 octets each wide).
  • Timestamp seconds and timestamp fraction, 4 octets each.
  • transit delay: nanoseconds spent in the node, 0 to 2^31-1, with a top overflow bit.
  • Namespace-specific data, 4 or 8 octets, meaning defined by the namespace.
  • queue depth and buffer occupancy: 4 octets, with implementation-specific semantics.
  • Checksum Complement: lets a node keep a UDP checksum correct without recomputing it.
  • Opaque State Snapshot: a variable-length field with a 24-bit Schema ID, interpreted per namespace.

The RFC defines syntax and mostly avoids semantics, so no units are given for fields such as queue depth. Systems that analyze the data handle unit conversion.
sections.eli5: Each stop fills in a short form: who am I, which doors did the postcard use, what time was it and how long did it wait. If a stop cannot answer a question, it writes all ones to say so.

sections.title: Proof of Transit and Edge-to-Edge
sections.content:
The Proof of Transit (POT) Option-Type supports verifying that traffic took a defined path, including service function chains. Two items go in the packet: PktID, a unique packet identifier, and Cumulative, which each node updates according to a verification algorithm. How nodes process them is outside this document. The only type defined, POT-Type 0, carries a 16-octet data field made of a 64-bit PktID and a 64-bit Cumulative.

The Edge-to-Edge (E2E) Option-Type carries data added by the encapsulating node and read by the decapsulating node. Transit nodes MAY process it but MUST NOT modify it. Its 16-bit E2E-Type bit field defines a 64-bit sequence number (bit 0) or a 32-bit one (bit 1), never both, used to detect loss, reordering or duplication within a deployment-defined "packet group", plus timestamp seconds (bit 2) and fraction (bit 3) for the time the packet entered the IOAM-Domain.

IANA created an "In Situ OAM (IOAM)" registry group with seven registries, including 128 Option-Type code points. New values mostly go through IETF Review. Namespace-IDs from 0x8000 up use Expert Review.
sections.eli5: Proof of transit is a stamp card: each stop adds its stamp so the finish line can check the whole route was followed. Edge-to-edge is a note that only the first and last post office read, like a numbered ticket to spot lost cards.

sections.title: Timestamp Formats
sections.content:
Timestamp fields use one of three 64-bit formats, split into a 32-bit seconds half and a 32-bit fraction half. The seconds field carries the 32 most significant bits and the fraction field the 32 least significant bits. The management plane decides which format is in use, and nodes are assumed to be synchronized.

  • PTP truncated: seconds and nanoseconds since the PTP epoch, 1 nanosecond resolution.
  • NTP 64-bit: seconds and a fraction in units of 2^(-32) second, roughly 233 picoseconds.
  • POSIX-based: seconds and microseconds since the POSIX epoch.

All three wrap every 2^32 seconds, about 136 years. The RFC notes that the next wraparound is in 2036 for NTP and 2106 for the other two.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of clock face a stop can use. The namespace says which one, so everyone reads the time the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points out that a successful attack on an OAM protocol can hide real failures or invent fake ones. Any node on the path can tamper with IOAM data or inject packets carrying bogus IOAM options.

  • Reconnaissance: IOAM data can reveal paths, performance, queue states and buffer occupancy, and more so if it leaks out of the IOAM-Domain.
  • Denial of service: an attacker can add IOAM headers to burn resources, or grow packets past the MTU so they fragment or drop. Corrupted POT data makes verification fail even on the right path.
  • Time attacks: attacking a time protocol can compromise timestamp data.
  • Misuse: compromised nodes could repurpose fields as a covert channel.

The key requirement: any specification that carries IOAM-Data-Fields in an encapsulating protocol MUST provide a mechanism for cryptographic integrity protection of those fields. The RFC leans on limited domains, where the operator controls and trusts all devices, and expects policies that stop IOAM traffic from leaving the domain.
sections.eli5: If someone scribbles in the travel diary, you could be fooled about what happened. So the rules say the diary must be sealed, and it should stay inside the building.

fields.desc: Set to zero by the encapsulating node; ignored by transit nodes.
